title: Chunky garter lap throw
subtitle: A fast single-panel lap throw in chunky wool on 6 mm needles.
excerpt: A 100 by 120 cm lap throw worked flat in garter stitch on 6 mm needles using approximately 600 g of chunky wool. Chunky weight and a large needle make this the fastest blanket in the collection: the throw knits up in a fraction of the time a DK blanket takes.
sourceNotes: Chunky-weight lap throws are a modern application of the single-panel garter construction documented in Weldon's Practical Knitter (1880s). The garter-stitch-flat technique is unchanged; the yarn weight and needle size reflect contemporary chunky-weight standards (Craft Yarn Council CYC 5 / UK chunky).

knitting.gaugeText: 14 sts × 28 rows = 10 × 10 cm in garter stitch on 6 mm needles, unblocked.

glossaryTerms.definition: A yarn weight class rated CYC 5 by the Craft Yarn Council, equivalent to UK chunky or heavy-worsted. Typically knits to 12 to 15 stitches per 10 cm on 6 to 8 mm needles. Produces a dense, warm fabric that knits up quickly.

content.text: A single-panel rectangle worked flat in garter stitch on 6 mm needles in
chunky-weight
wool, finishing at 100 cm wide by 120 cm long.

Single-panel construction was chosen because chunky yarn has bulk enough to drape well in one flat sheet, with no seaming required. At chunky weight on 6 mm needles this throw knits far faster than the DK blankets in the collection: the cast-on row is only 140 stitches and each garter ridge is two quick rows of knitting. Budget about 600 g (about 720 m / 790 yards) of chunky wool or a chunky wool blend. Buy all the yarn at once in matched dye lots; a blanket of this size draws from four or five skeins and a dye-lot shift is visible against chunky fabric. Drapes over a sofa end or across the lap in an armchair; folds to a manageable rectangle for a bag.
What you need

items.name: Yarn
items.qty: 600 g (about 720 m / 790 yards) of chunky-weight wool or wool blend
items.substitutions: 100% British wool chunky, chunky merino, or a wool-acrylic blend at CYC 5. Avoid acrylic-only yarn if the throw will be steam-blocked: acrylic distorts under steam and does not recover.

items.name: Needles
items.qty: 6 mm (UK 4 / US 10) circular needle, 100 cm or longer, or a long straight needle

content.text: Gauge

14 stitches and 28 rows to 10 cm over garter stitch on 6 mm needles, unblocked. Swatch a 20 cm square and measure the centre 10 cm. Chunky yarn is variable between brands: a CYC 5 yarn can run anywhere from 12 to 16 stitches per 10 cm depending on the fibre and twist. Matching the stitch gauge matters more than matching the row gauge for a blanket worked to a measured length.

If your stitch gauge is 12 per 10 cm instead of 14, the 140-stitch cast-on will produce a blanket about 117 cm wide instead of 100 cm. If your gauge is 16 per 10 cm, the width will be about 87 cm. Adjust the cast-on count to hit 100 cm: multiply 100 cm by your actual stitch gauge per 10 cm to get the target cast-on number, then round to an even stitch count.
Stitches used
Pattern
Cast-on

Using the long-tail cast-on, cast on 140 stitches. Long-tail tail length: (6 × 140) / 10 + 15 = 84 + 15 = 99 cm. Measure 110 cm of tail before starting; round up to 130 cm to leave a safe margin. A chunky-yarn cast-on takes more tail per stitch than a DK cast-on because each stitch sits around a wider needle.
Body
Knit every row until the throw measures 120 cm from the cast-on edge. At gauge that is 336 rows, but measuring is more accurate.
When you set this aside, jot the current row or measure the length. Picking up a garter throw is simple because every row is a knit row.
Stitch count check-ins
At row 168 (about 60 cm): count across the needle. You should have 140 stitches. At row 333 (about 119 cm): count again before the final cast-off row.
Common faults

Blanket narrowing towards one end: tension tightened as the session progressed, or the yarn is splitting on the needle and some stitches were worked tighter than others. Chunky yarn with a low twist can split around the needle; use smooth-tipped needles and check that the whole stitch is on the needle before each knit.

Dropped stitch runs visible in chunky garter: dropped stitches run quickly in chunky yarn because the stitches are large and the fabric is loose. Count every 20 rows and address any run immediately by picking the dropped stitch up through the garter ridges with a crochet hook.

Dye-lot shift visible mid-throw: skeins came from different dye lots. Alternate two skeins every two rows to average any drift. With chunky yarn the shift is particularly visible because the yarn is thick and the colour difference reads at a greater distance.
Cast-off

Cast off knitwise with a loose, even tension. Chunky yarn benefits from an extra-loose cast-off because the edge will otherwise pull in and be noticeably narrower than the body. Work each stitch deliberately without rushing.
Finishing

Weave in both ends with a blunt tapestry needle suitable for chunky yarn, running each tail at least 5 cm along a garter ridge and changing direction once. Trim. Garter stitch in chunky wool lies flat without any pressing. A very light steam hold will smooth the edges if they wave slightly.
Care

Hand wash in cool water if the yarn is 100% non-superwash wool. Machine wash on a gentle 30-degree cycle only if the yarn label specifies superwash. Lay flat to dry; a chunky-weight throw is too heavy to hang without distortion when wet. Allow several hours for a throw this size to dry completely.
What to try next

From a plain chunky garter throw, the natural next project is a striped chunky throw: the same construction, two colours, carrying the yarn up the side. Because chunky stripes are physically larger than DK stripes, four-row chunky stripes produce a bolder graphic than four-row DK stripes. After that, a chunky seed-stitch throw adds purl stitches to the alternating row and produces a denser, slightly shorter fabric at the same needle size.
